title: The colour wheel, and why there is more than one — Image Wiki
text:
The colour wheel, and why there is more than one
  A ring of hues in spectral order, closed at the join by colours no wavelength can make. It is a working model, not a picture of light — and different jobs need different wheels, which is why they disagree about what sits opposite what.

  
    Termcolour wheel / hue circle
    Also calledhue circle, colour circle, hue ring, RYB wheel, CMY wheel, RGB wheel
    Not the same ashue circle vs colour solid, artists' wheel vs printers' wheel, wheel position vs mixing behaviour
    Read8 min
  

  
    
      On this page
      
        Why the wheel is a model and not a measurementFour wheels, four jobsThe practical consequenceCommon mistakes
      
    
  

  Find a strong magenta on your screen — the pink-purple of a highlighter pen. Now go and find that colour in a rainbow.
It is not there. A rainbow runs red, orange, yellow, green, blue, violet, and stops. Magenta appears at no wavelength of light, and neither does crimson, nor most of what you would call plain red. Your eye makes those hues out of the two ends of the spectrum arriving together.
That is the first thing to know about a colour wheel: the ring only closes because your visual system supplies the joint. Bend the spectrum until its ends touch and you are left with a wedge to fill, and nothing in physics fills it.

Left, the spectrum as a prism gives it to you: a strip with two ends, 300 nanometres apart. Above it sit three hues you use every day — purple, magenta, crimson — and they are on no part of that strip.
Right, the same strip bent until 400 nm meets 700 nm. Measured in perceptual hue angle, the spectral colours only account for about 286° of the circle. The remaining 74° — roughly a fifth of every colour wheel ever printed — is the hatched wedge, and no single wavelength produces any of it. Colour science even names those hues backwards, by the wavelength of the hue opposite them: a magenta is written c560, meaning "the complement of 560 nm".


Why the wheel is a model and not a measurement
Newton drew the first hue circle, and he drew it for a specific job: to explain why mixing two coloured lights gives a duller result than either one alone. The circle predicted that loss. The rule still holds and is worth memorising — the further apart two colours sit on the hue circle, the duller their mixture — and Handprint calls the effect the saturation cost.
Notice what that means. The wheel was invented as a calculator for one question. Ask it a different question and it may answer wrongly, because nothing guarantees a single arrangement of hues serves every purpose.


Harris, 1776: red sits opposite green
Munsell: red sits opposite blue-green


Left: Moses Harris, the "Prismatic" plate from The Natural System of Colours, 1776 — a hand-coloured engraving in 18 sectors, on cream paper with brown foxing across the blue and blue-purple sectors at left. Right: the Munsell hue-notation circle, after A. H. Munsell (1858–1918) — a line diagram, 40 spokes and a 100-step rim, with no colour on it at all. Both public domain. Read Harris for positions rather than exact hues; the pigments are 250 years old.
Read the labels and the two plates contradict each other. Harris puts RED at twelve o'clock and Green at six: red opposite green, orange opposite blue, yellow opposite purple. Look at his centre — three overlapping triangles, crimson, grey-blue and yellow, meeting in solid black. That is the red-yellow-blue claim, drawn.
Munsell puts R at twelve o'clock and BG at six, with N for neutral at the hub. Red is opposite blue-green, yellow opposite purple-blue, and green opposite red-purple. This is not a rounding difference. Harris's wheel records how paints were believed to mix; Munsell's is built from psychophysical measurement of how far apart people judge colour chips to look. One is a painter's object, the other a measurement notation — and the notation needs no ink to do its job.


Four wheels, four jobs
The artists' red-yellow-blue wheel is a pigment convention, first stated by the printer Jakob Le Blon in 1725 and drawn by Harris in the 1760s. It answers: which three tubes shall I buy? It gets mixing wrong, and the reason is physical. A red paint reflects almost no short-wavelength light and a blue paint almost no long-wavelength light, so neither can supply what the other lacks; Harris himself conceded that "red and blue will not make a fine purple, which every painter knows". Blue also lacks the middle-wavelength green needed to mix a strong green with yellow.
The printers' cyan-magenta-yellow set fixes exactly that, and it is the one to reach for when the question is subtractive mixing — inks, dyes, paint. Magenta was only standardised as a printing primary in 1934. It is still not complete: CMYK cannot reach many saturated oranges, violets, blues and yellow-greens, which is why six- and seven-ink presses exist.
The additive red-green-blue set describes lights: screens, projectors, stage lamps. It answers nothing about paint. And it has its own hole — three real primaries can never mix every colour, because the set of all visible colours is bounded by a curve, not a triangle. The primaries that can explain every colour sit outside that curve and are therefore invisible. Handprint's summary is the one to keep: every primary is either imaginary or imperfect.
Perceptual hue circles — Munsell, CIELAB, CIECAM — do not assume a set of primaries at all. Hue is measured as an angle, and the spacing comes out uneven: there is fine discrimination around yellow and cyan, coarse discrimination in the greens and at the spectrum ends. These circles answer "what will this look like next to that", and they say nothing directly about what happens in the mixing tray.



M.-E. Chevreul, 1er cercle chromatique … renfermant les couleurs franches, plate engraved by Digeon and printed by Lemercier for J.-B. Baillière et Fils, Paris, 1864. Science History Institute via Wikimedia Commons; public domain.
Seventy-two hand-coloured sectors, each divided from the next by a hairline of bare paper, with named cartouches and numbered steps around the rim — industrial precision, ninety years after Harris. Find the names: VERT at the very top, ROUGE at the very bottom, JAUNE upper right, ORANGE lower right, VIOLET lower left, BLEU upper left.
Now follow the diameters. Rouge is still opposite vert, orange still opposite bleu, jaune still opposite violet. Ninety years of refinement inside the red-yellow-blue tradition did not move one cardinal point. So the disagreement in the pair above is not sloppiness on either side — it is two traditions answering two different questions, each self-consistent.


Handprint is a useful witness here because he publishes his own wheel and has revised it once already: the 1999 and 2006 versions differ "in their chroma scaling of all colors, and in the spacing and visual complements assigned to blue and violet colors". Both are built from spectrophotometer readings of ninety real watercolour pigments. If the author of a measured wheel moves blue and violet after seven years, you are looking at a model under revision, not a fact about light.
The practical consequence
Which wheel you use decides what counts as "opposite".

start hereultramarine blueopposite isorangeArtists’ wheelred, yellow, blue as primariesHarris 1766, Chevreul 1839start hereultramarine blueopposite isyellowPrinters’ wheelcyan, magenta, yellow as primariesCMYK, standardised 1934start hereultramarine blueopposite isyellow greenPerceptual hue circlehue measured, not assumedCIELAB / Munsell / CIECAM

The same swatch of ultramarine blue sits at twelve o'clock on all three wheels. Only the wheel changes.
The artists' wheel sends you to orange. The printers' wheel sends you to yellow. The perceptual circle, measuring the blue at hue angle 296° and reading off 116°, sends you to a yellow-green — which is what Handprint gives as ultramarine's visual complement. Three answers, all correct for their own question, and no two of them the same colour.


So "use the opposite colour" is not yet an instruction. Opposite on what? Until you say, the sentence has not told you which of those three colours to pick — and they are far enough apart that the choice changes the picture. See Complementary colours for what each kind of opposite is actually good for.
Common mistakes

"The colour wheel shows the colours of light." About a fifth of it shows colours light cannot make on its own. The ring is closed by your eye.
"Red, yellow and blue are the primary colours." They are a convention from the 1700s, chosen for the pigments then available. They mix dull purples and dull greens for a physical reason.
"There is a correct colour wheel." There is a correct wheel for a question. Handprint, who built one of the most careful wheels in existence, says flatly that there is no objective colour wheel and no best palette.
"Two colours next to each other on the wheel will mix well." Adjacent hues mix with the least saturation cost, which is not the same as mixing well. A wheel cannot show mixing accurately at all — you cannot draw one where every mixing line is straight, and no rearranging of the hues fixes it.
"Position on the wheel tells me how a paint behaves." It tells you hue. Two paints at the same hue can differ enormously in chroma, lightness, opacity and tinting strength — see Hue, value and chroma.


Which wheel is this person using?

Find red. What is directly opposite it? Green means a red-yellow-blue wheel; blue-green or cyan means a printers' or perceptual one.
Are the hues evenly spaced? Even spacing is a drawing convention. Measured circles come out uneven.
Is there a magenta on it? There has to be, and no wavelength made it.
Ask what the wheel is being used for. Buying paint, predicting a mixture, or choosing what goes next to what are three different questions, and no one wheel answers all three.

              Hue, value and chroma
              A colour is not one thing. It is three independent dials — which colour it is, how light it is, and how far it sits from grey — and most arguments about colour are two people turning different dials.
            
          
        
          
            
              Complementary colours
              The pair of colours that cancel each other. There are two different pairs answering to that name — the one that mixes to grey and the one your eye pairs — and they are almost never the same colour.
            
          
        
          
            
              How to choose colours
              A practical order of operations for picking colours — decide the job, choose on all three dials, then set the areas — and an honest account of why the named schemes explain much less than they claim.
            
          
        
          
            
              The colour of the light
              What you see is the object's own colour multiplied by the light's colour — and your brain quietly divides the light back out, which is why a white shirt looks white everywhere.
